cim: How to Build an Artificial Intelligence Revolution for All
cim_eredeti: How to Build an Artificial Intelligence Revolution for All
szoveg_eredeti:
The most important flashpoint in the debate over the future of artificial intelligence for both business and political leaders is: What is the impact of the technology on working Americans? Over the long term, AI’s promise will be measured not by the scale of its investment, disruption, or productivity, but by the apportionment across America of the value it creates. It is vital that both Republicans and Democrats unite with the business and investment community to provide a solution that is acceptable to the majority of Americans.

During the Midterm elections, all but one of 41 propositions to build data centers failed. In my view, this was not a reflection of specific concerns about the data centers, but of overall rejection of the current trajectory of AI growth. Plus, without the extraordinary growth in AI investment, it is likely that overall GDP growth of America would be negative. If AI development is stopped or seriously slowed down, our economy could slide backward.

To date, both business and government have failed miserably in making the case for widespread benefits from AI. Right now, Americans only see that the tech bros, Trump, and his allies get richer from AI, while the consequences for ordinary Americans seem more dire.

The solution must be constructed and implemented by business and government working together.

At the Council for Inclusive Capitalism’s roundtable alongside the UN General Assembly in September, executives, investors and policymakers offered useful suggestions. Our consultations with Council members over several months in 2026 resulted in a consensus that workers must be involved in how AI is deployed in order to reverse the groundswell against the technology and turn AI’s potential into lasting value for all.

In July, I wrote that AI should give rise to an ownership economy, in which workers share in the wealth the technology creates. In many ways, Elon Musk’s promise to gift one share of SpaceX to every American child under the age of 18 could be a start. The same is true of Anthropic’s “public benefit” fund, composed of 5% of its shares, which would be valued at nearly $75 billion.

That being said, the long-term viability of AI will not be measured in individual acts of philanthropy. Fortunately, there are several ways we could forge a better path today.

First, companies must engage employees to identify business needs, test AI applications, and fold them into daily routines. This makes practical sense. People doing the work know where a process breaks down and where human judgment cannot be replaced.

The company’s part is to invest in skills tied to real openings, give people time to experiment, and help managers redesign workflows. Time saved only creates value when it becomes better service, new products, and opportunities for customers and employees.

Second, employers have to prepare current staff for new responsibilities while keeping a route open for young people who are just starting out. AI is changing tasks, skills and hiring all at once. Companies that treat headcount reductions as the primary measure of AI’s success risk losing the people who understand both the technology and the business.

Employers, educators and policymakers can build routes in and up through apprenticeships, paid placements, internal mobility and structured learning alongside seasoned colleagues.

And third, we must bring public and private investment together or else the burden of transitioning to the AI era will fall unevenly. McKinsey projects that lower-wage workers are 7.6 times as likely as higher-wage workers to need a new occupation, and they often have the least capacity to retrain or absorb a temporary loss of income. Support has to reach the people facing the steepest barriers.

Some companies are acting. Verizon, for instance, committed $70 million to AI Skills for America in September, combining $50 million in new funding with its existing $20 million fund for departing workers, and pairing free training with community coaching through partners such as Goodwill Industries.

Government has its own tools. Workforce Pell, enacted in 2025 and now in effect, lets workers use federal Pell Grants for short-term job training. Proposals in Congress would go further. Senator Mark Kelly’s Make AI Work for Americans Act would create a federal AI Horizon Fund, financed by the companies that profit most from AI, to pay for training and support for displaced workers. Senators Mark Warner and Josh Hawley have introduced bipartisan legislation requiring companies to report AI-related job losses so that policymakers can see the labor-market effects as they happen. None has yet become law.

What is good for workers is good for business. The choices companies make about AI in the coming months will shape both their competitiveness and their employees’ prospects, and the two are more closely tied than the layoff debate suggests.

The Council’s next phase will connect company experience with public policy, identify what works, and examine where public and private efforts can close gaps together. Inclusive capitalism has always been a practical idea: build lasting business value by expanding people’s ability to contribute to, and share in, economic success.

We do not need certainty about AI’s final impact to act. Workers should help shape the transition and share in the prosperity they help create.
